name: document-message
intent: Transfer a single self-contained data document between applications over a message channel so that the receiver, not the sender, decides what the data means and what to do with it: the document's content is the contract, its timing is not.
problem: An application must hand a data structure to another application (or to several) across a boundary, but the sender neither knows nor should prescribe what the receiver will do with it. Sending an instruction (Command Message) or a timing-bound notification (Event Message) imports the wrong semantics, while file transfer or a shared database couple the two applications far more tightly than the data exchange requires.
context: Application-to-application integration over messaging, where the payload is one structured unit of data - a customer record, an order, an invoice, a measurement batch - and the content of that document matters while the exact moment it is sent and received does not. Typical conditions: producer and consumer are deployed, versioned and scaled independently; several consumers may need the same data for different purposes; the transport is a message channel with store-and-forward or guaranteed delivery rather than a synchronous call; and both sides can agree on a wire format plus a schema for the document.
benefits: Decoupling of data transfer from behavior: the sender publishes data and every receiver decides locally whether to apply, store, transform or ignore it, so adding a consumer never changes the producer.
One document serves many receivers: the same published record can feed a warehouse, a billing run and a search index without the producer knowing about any of them.
Transport and format independence: the document travels over any channel and can be encoded as JSON, XML, protobuf or a fixed binary layout as long as both sides agree on the schema.
Store-and-forward robustness: because timing is not part of the contract, documents can be queued, retried and replayed while a consumer is down or being redeployed.
Natural fit for batch- and delta-style integration: bulk data shipments, master-data replication and reporting feeds are plain documents instead of remote calls.
Testability: a document is data, so producers can be exercised against fixture documents and consumers against recorded ones without a live counterpart.
tradeoffs: The receiver decides means the sender cannot enforce processing: without adding Request-Reply and a Correlation Identifier the producer neither controls nor learns what happened to the document.

The document schema becomes a shared contract: every field addition, rename or type change is a cross-team change, so versioning, schema registries and tolerant readers become mandatory rather than optional.

Validation and error handling move to the consumer: malformed or semantically impossible documents arrive at runtime, and each endpoint needs its own validation plus an invalid-message or dead-letter path.

Timing is explicitly not part of the contract, so stale documents can be applied late or twice; business timestamps, message expiration for genuinely time-bound data and idempotent receivers are the compensating controls.

Payloads are large compared with commands or events - a whole data structure per message - which pressures broker size limits, memory and serialization CPU and eventually forces a Claim Check for big documents.

The wire format is an architectural decision: schema-first encodings buy compactness and typed contracts at the cost of a code-generation toolchain, while JSON buys reachability at the cost of bytes and type fidelity (numbers, dates, binary).
Behavior is data-dependent, so a document on a channel names no operation and operators must read consumer code to know what will happen to it, unlike a command message.

participants.responsibility: Owns the data and creates the document from its own state at the moment of sending; it knows the schema but not what any receiver will do with the data.
The single unit of data being transferred - one object or data structure that may itself decompose into smaller units; its content is what matters, not its arrival time.
The envelope: headers carrying identification, routing and format/version information, plus the document as the body on the channel.
Transports messages reliably, point-to-point for exactly one receiver or publish-subscribe for many; delivery semantics stay independent of document content.

Translates between the application's internal representation and the wire document, validates incoming documents and hands plain data to the receiver's logic, so domain model and messaging infrastructure stay unaware of each other.
Decides what the document means for it - apply, store, aggregate, forward or ignore - and owns the error path for documents it cannot use.

use_cases: Master- and reference-data replication: the system of record publishes customer, product or pricing documents that downstream systems replicate into their own stores, maintaining consistency without tight coupling.

Order, invoice and claim hand-off into a fulfilment, billing or settlement pipeline, where each stage picks the fields it needs from the same document without the producer knowing downstream stages exist.

Business-to-business exchange of trade documents (purchase order, despatch advice, invoice) in an agreed interchange format over a broker or partner gateway, where legal entities require non-repudiation and guaranteed delivery.
Data-platform ingestion: applications publish changed entities as documents so a lakehouse or search index can consume them without the producer knowing the target schema or infrastructure.

Telemetry and measurement batches from devices, agents or batch jobs that are collected centrally, archived and processed later; timing is not critical but completeness and ordering within a batch are.
Webhook and event-carried state transfer payloads, where a provider posts a resource representation and each subscriber decides independently how to react, cache, or store the data.

Change Data Capture (CDC) pipelines: database row changes captured via Debezium or similar tools are published as documents to Kafka or another broker, enabling zero-code integration between legacy systems and cloud-native microservices.

Data mesh data products: domain teams publish structured data products (customer profiles, transaction records) as versioned documents with explicit contracts, enabling federated data consumption across the enterprise with domain-owned SLAs.

Schema registry-backed integration: Avro- or Protobuf-encoded documents with schema IDs enable type-safe document exchange across services with automatic schema evolution support via backward/forward compatibility checks at the registry.

Financial reconciliation feeds: trading systems publish position, trade and settlement documents to a central reconciliation engine where each counterparty's version of the data is compared and discrepancies are flagged.
Healthcare record exchange: clinical systems exchange HL7 FHIR or custom clinical documents across institutional boundaries, where document immutability and audit trails are regulatory requirements.

IoT device state synchronization: edge devices publish full-state documents on a regular heartbeat interval; receiving services rebuild local replicas and detect anomalies from state deltas computed locally.

Healthcare integration engines: Mirth Connect (NextGen Connect) receives HL7 v2, X12 and DICOM clinical documents on channel source connectors with store-and-forward queuing, filters and transformers, letting each destination system decide how to apply the document.

Trading-partner EDI interchange: AS2 (RFC 4130) transports signed, encrypted X12/EDIFACT purchase orders, despatch advices and invoices over HTTP with signed MDN receipts, the canonical Document Message across legal-entity boundaries.

ESB document forwarding: WSO2 Micro Integrator implements the Document Message EIP as a proxy service that forwards the complete received document to a backend endpoint, which interprets the document and decides what operation it implies.
avoid_when: The sender must ensure that a specific operation happens: use a Command Message, plus Request-Reply when the result or a domain error has to come back.
Only the fact and the moment of a change matter: use an Event Message; the document's content would be ballast.
The data is needed synchronously inside the current request: a remote procedure invocation or a plain query is simpler and reports errors immediately.
The payload is too large or too sensitive to travel on the channel: use a Claim Check and send a reference instead.
Producer and consumer share a database and a deployment: a query or an in-process call replaces the whole messaging machinery.
The document would be a disguised operation (fields naming commands, expected side effects): that is a Command Message with worse readability.
anti_patterns: Command in document clothing: a document whose fields encode an operation the receiver is expected to perform, hiding intent and leaking sender behavior into every consumer.
Publishing internal domain or ORM entities as the wire document, so every internal refactor silently changes the contract.
Unlimited payloads: shipping whole tables, blobs or full history as one document instead of using a Claim Check.
Consumer-side guessing: parsing documents with implicit assumptions about optional fields and no version handling, so newer producer versions are silently misread.
Fire-and-forget for business-critical data: no delivery guarantee, no idempotency, no invalid-message channel, and no answer to where a record went.
Using the message channel as the system of record: treating in-flight documents as the authoritative store instead of using a message store or a database.
Schema breaking changes without migration plan: removing fields, changing types, or renaming elements without a versioned topic strategy breaks existing consumers.
Non-idempotent document processing: assuming every delivered document is unique when at-least-once delivery may redeliver the same document multiple times.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: transferring data is separated from deciding what to do with it.
Information hiding: consumers see a published document contract, never the producer's internal model.
Loose coupling through an explicit, versioned contract (a canonical data model) instead of shared runtime types.
Single responsibility at the boundary: endpoints own mapping, validation and error routing; domain code stays messaging-agnostic.
Design for evolution: contracts tolerate additive change - new fields optional, unknown fields ignored, mandatory fields never repurposed.
Schema-first contract: define the document schema in a registry before implementation; never derive the wire contract from internal classes.
Idempotent by design: consumers must handle duplicate delivery gracefully; use a stable deduplication key stored atomically with business state.
best_practices: Design an explicit document schema (IDL, JSON Schema, Avro, or Protobuf), keep it in its own artifact under version control, and never derive the wire contract implicitly from internal classes.

Version every document (schema ID, version header, or format indicator) and evolve additively; make consumers tolerant readers that skip unknown fields, and producers that omit fields with zero/default values.
Validate every incoming document at the endpoint and route rejects to an invalid-message or dead-letter channel; do not fail silently or allow malformed documents into business logic.

Choose the encoding per document type: compact schema-first formats (Avro, Protobuf) for high-volume or typed contracts; JSON for reachability, debuggability and human readability; measure serialization cost before committing.

Keep documents self-describing with enough metadata (document type, version, source system, timestamp) to be interpreted without a shared runtime, and bind the document kind to a datatype channel so receivers know the type up front.

Configure delivery guarantees explicitly: at-least-once for documents where loss is unacceptable; exactly-once where supported (broker-based deduplication); and pair every non-idempotent consumer with a stable deduplication key stored atomically with the business write.

Send a reference (Claim Check) rather than a full document when the payload exceeds broker size limits or carries large blobs; store the payload in external storage (S3, Azure Blob, GCS) and pass only the reference on the channel.
Do not encode behavior in the document: when the receiver must execute a specific operation, use a Command Message — a document that encodes an intended action is a Command Message in disguise.

Use a schema registry (Confluent, Apicurio, AWS Glue Schema Registry) to manage schema versions, enforce compatibility rules, and prevent breaking changes from being deployed without a migration path.

Configure schema compatibility mode per document type: BACKWARD (new schema reads old data) is the safe default; BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE when all historical versions must remain readable; FULL when deployment order cannot be controlled; AVRO and Protobuf require different compatibility semantics.

For Avro: represent optional fields with union ["null", <type>] and explicit default values; for Protobuf: use the optional keyword, set reserved retired field numbers, and never reuse numbers from removed fields.

Align with data mesh principles: treat published documents as data products with explicit contracts, versioned schemas, domain ownership, SLAs, discoverability metadata (catalog tags), and a clear consumers list.

For CDC-driven document messages: emit the complete changed entity state as the document, not just the delta; include key fields (primary key, change timestamp, operation type) to enable downstream ordering, deduplication, and reconstruction.
Monitor document processing metrics: consumer lag, dead-letter queue depth, schema compatibility violations, and end-to-end latency; set alerts on error rate thresholds and queue depth anomalies.
Document the semantic meaning and ownership of each field in the schema spec; use a consistent naming convention (camelCase, snake_case) across the contract and enforce it in CI.

Implement circuit breakers on the consumer side: when a document consumer is degraded, the message broker should throttle or pause delivery rather than letting a backlog of unprocessable documents grow.

Use content enrichers or outbox patterns when the producer does not naturally hold all the fields consumers need: rather than reaching back into the producer, pre-enrich the document at the source or use a separate enrichment step.

For high-throughput document streams, batch documents into a single transport message (one-to-many via a wrapping envelope) only when consumers can efficiently split and route them; profile before adopting.
Version the topic or channel alongside the schema: a new schema major version should map to a new topic or a routing rule in the broker so old and new consumers can coexist during migration.
